hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Brand new study just dropped (published Oct 29, 2026 in Frontiers in Pharmacology). 
A massive new analysis from two of the world’s largest biomedical databases just linked statin use to roughly double the risk of dementia.

Researchers looked at the All of Us Research Program (83,355 adults, including over 31,000 statin users, followed through 2023) and the UK Biobank (173,282 adults, including nearly 44,000 statin users). After balancing groups for age, BMI, APOE status, comorbidities, and other factors using inverse probability of treatment weighting, statin users showed adjusted hazard ratios of 2.22 (All of Us) and 2.54 (UK Biobank) for incident dementia.

The association held across Alzheimer’s disease, vascular dementia, and other subtypes. High-intensity statins carried an additional ~14% higher risk compared with moderate-to-low intensity therapy. Incidence rates were higher in the discovery cohort (64.9 vs 30.7 per 10,000 person-years) than in the replication cohort, but the relative increase was consistent.

In an exploratory mediation analysis, a modest portion (8.2%) of the association appeared to run through lower levels of coenzyme Q7—a protein involved in CoQ10 biosynthesis. Lower COQ7 was itself linked to higher dementia odds. The pathway through LDL-C was not statistically significant. The authors note this is hypothesis-generating and that direct CoQ10 was not measured.

This is observational data, not a randomized trial, so it cannot prove causation. Residual confounding (including why people were prescribed statins) remains possible, and the literature on statins and cognition has been mixed. Still, the scale, the replication across two independent cohorts, the intensity-dependent pattern, and the COQ7 signal make it hard to ignore.

This is the kind of result that makes people who have been skeptical of long-term statin use for primary prevention sit up and take notice—especially given the CoQ10 connection many clinicians have quietly acknowledged for years.

The full paper is open access: https://t.co/dEanGT17LV
hits.draft_en:

hits.name: Ken D Berry MD

Dr. Hyman is right, and the data behind it is old enough that every doctor should know it by now. Blood sugar is the last thing to break.

The Whitehall II study followed 6,538 British civil servants who did not have diabetes, for a median of 9.7 years. 505 of them got diabetes, and the researchers went back and tracked what their labs did before the diagnosis.

Fasting glucose crept up slowly, then rose steeply starting 3 years before diagnosis, from 5.79 to 7.40 mmol/L. That is about 104 to 133 mg/dL. Insulin sensitivity fell steeply during the 5 years before diagnosis. Beta-cell output actually rose between years 4 and 3 before diagnosis, then fell.

The authors wrote that they saw "changes in glucose concentrations, insulin sensitivity, and insulin secretion as much as 3-6 years before diagnosis of diabetes."

So the pancreas was working overtime for years while the standard glucose number still looked fine. That is hyperinsulinemia, and few doctors ever check for it. A fasting glucose by itself is the late warning.

Ask your doctor for a fasting insulin test. If it is high, Low-carb/Keto/Carnivore is how you bring it down.

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text:
I'm happy to see these results from the FLOWPROMOTE RCT, showing that lipid-modifying pharmacotherapy led to plaque regression in the majority of patients over the course of 18 months. 

And I think this provides an excellent moment to interject nuance, where there's generally a tendency to become more polarized.

First, because I know it's of interest, and often misrepresented, bear in mind that at no point have I ever said lipid-lowering medications are universally bad, nor have I provided individualized prescriptive recommendations. 

Because, as with almost everything in health, it's all about individualized risk-benefit analysis.

And the data suggest larger absolute benefits in those who are at HIGH cardiovascular risk, including those with confirmed cardiovascular disease, or features of metabolic syndrome.

The patients here were in said category
👉 Half with hypertension
👉 ~60% being former smokers
👉 Overweight on average
👉 Diagnosed coronary artery disease (e.g., coronary stenosis greater than 50% 👉 per inclusion criteria).

🚨They also had high baseline plaque (Baseline mean/median: 375 / 316 mm3)

nb: Keto-CTA comparison: (mean/median: 51/25 mm3)

(Though I won't get on a soap box about the 'noise floor' here.)

Bottom line, these were high risk people and the perfect subjects for this trial.

Conclusion?

The data show benefits with respect to cardiovascular health in this population.

That’s not a surprise, although the regression (assuming the reads are reliable...topic for another time), are impressive.

All I would caution against is extrapolating from this high-risk population to the much broader and unsubstantiated conclusion that aggressive lipid-lowering therapy is necessary for everyone as a preventive measure. 

That’s not dogmatic. It’s logic and reason.

As a recent complementary perspective case in point, the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology paper (PMID: 42533703), looking at interactions between HDL and ApoB, found for those with high HDL (just one marker of good metabolic health), there was no observed relationship between ApoB and 10-year cardiovascular disease risk. And that is just one marker. 

In every circumstance we see here, the context matters, whether you're prescribing pharmacotherapy or trying a diet.

Bottom line: These are very positive results. 

And beyond anything, I'm very happy for the patients whose outcomes and cardiovascular risk are improving.

I think that's something we should all celebrate. Fair enough?

📖 Primary reference: JAMA Cardio. Oct 30, 2026. doi: 10.1001/jamacardio.2026.4788

Tucker is right. Low-fat advice is one of the ways people end up having their gallbladder taken out, and there is a randomized study that shows it.

Hepatology, 1996. Obese patients on rapid weight loss liquid diets were randomized to one of two plans. One had less than 2 grams of fat a day. The other had 30 grams of fat a day, including one 10 gram fat meal to make the gallbladder empty.

Both groups lost 22% of their body weight.

On the near fat-free plan, the gallbladder emptied only 35%, compared with their maximum emptying of 66%. The fat meal gave full emptying.

Gallstones formed in 4 of 6 people on the near fat-free plan and 0 of 7 on the plan with fat. That difference "resulted in premature study termination for ethical reasons." They had to stop the study early.

The authors concluded that gallstone risk during rapid weight loss "may be reduced by maintenance of gallbladder emptying with a small amount of dietary fat."

That was 30 years ago, and low-fat is still what a lot of people get told after a gallbladder attack. Few doctors ever read this one. Eat real fat with your meals.

Ken Berry on low-fat diets and gallstones.

A 1996 trial in Hepatology put people on rapid weight-loss diets. One group had under 2 grams of fat a day, the other 30 grams.

Small study, old study. But if you're cutting weight fast, a bit of real fat with meals keeps the gallbladder working. Talk to your doctor before going near fat-free.

In a quiet lab at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, psychologist Robert Sorge and his team set out to test something that defied the usual medical script for knee osteoarthritis: instead of more pills or surgery, could the food on the plate itself turn down the pain? 

Knee OA is the most common form of arthritis—roughly 15% of Americans deal with it, and the grinding pain in weight-bearing joints often steals mobility and quality of life. Standard treatments (NSAIDs, opioids, injections) bring side effects that can cascade into more medications. Sorge, director of UAB’s PAIN Collective, hypothesized that refined carbohydrates were fueling oxidative stress and inflammation in ways that amplified functional pain—the kind that makes standing, walking, or climbing stairs feel punishing. A low-fat approach (the long-standing dietary default) might not be the answer.

The Experiment
In a randomized controlled pilot study published in Pain Medicine (2019/2020), 21 adults aged 65–75 (9 men, 12 women) with knee OA were assigned for 12 weeks to one of three paths: a low-carbohydrate diet (LCD), a low-fat diet (LFD), or continuing their usual eating (control). 

The LCD group started by dropping total (not just net) carbs to about ≤20 g/day for the first three weeks, then up to ≤40 g if needed. Protein and fat were unrestricted—think meats, eggs, limited non-starchy vegetables, nuts, seeds, butter, and oils. No calorie counting focused on weight loss alone. The low-fat group followed conventional lower-fat guidance. Every three weeks, the team measured self-reported pain, quality of life, and depression. They also tracked functional pain with real-world tasks: repeated chair stands, timed walks, and repeated knee stimulation to measure how much pain the movements themselves provoked. Blood was drawn before and after to check oxidative stress markers and the adipokine leptin.

What Happened
Both the low-carb and low-fat groups lost weight and BMI, as expected. But only the low-carb group showed clear, significant drops in pain intensity and unpleasantness during the functional tasks, plus better self-reported pain scores and quality-of-life improvements. The low-fat and usual-diet groups did not match those gains. The LCD also uniquely lowered oxidative stress and leptin levels; the drop in oxidative stress tracked with reduced functional pain. 
Sorge put it plainly: “Our work shows people can reduce their pain with a change in diet.” He added that weight loss alone did not explain the relief—“the quality of the diet and types of foods consumed have more to do with pain reduction than weight loss.” Diet would not “cure” the arthritis, but it could dial pain down so it no longer wrecked daily life, without the side-effect spiral of drugs. 

The Takeaway
It was a small pilot (21 people), so larger trials have followed, including work exploring diverse populations and comparing low-carb approaches to USDA-style diets. But the core finding landed: for these older adults with knee OA, cutting refined carbohydrates outperformed cutting fat on the measures that mattered most for living with the pain. The mechanism pointed toward lower oxidative stress and inflammation rather than the scale alone.
The story is a reminder that sometimes the most direct path to quieter joints is not another prescription—it’s what ends up on the plate.

A high A1C doesn't always mean high blood sugar. This matters, because A1C is the number most people and many doctors rely on to judge glucose control and to diagnose diabetes.

A1C measures how much glucose has attached to hemoglobin, the protein inside red blood cells. Glucose sticks to hemoglobin slowly and steadily, so the longer a red blood cell stays in circulation, the more glucose builds up on it. That's why A1C is treated as a two- to three-month average of blood sugar.

That also means A1C depends on more than glucose. It depends on how old the red blood cells are. When iron is low, the body makes fewer new red blood cells, so the cells already in circulation are older on average. Older cells have had more time to collect glucose, and A1C goes up even though blood sugar hasn't changed.

When researchers pooled the studies in adults without diabetes, iron deficiency, with or without anemia, was consistently linked to a higher A1C. Some other types of anemia, where red blood cells are destroyed faster than usual, can do the opposite and make A1C look falsely low.

This matters most for people who are more likely to be low in iron, including menstruating women, pregnant women, frequent blood donors, and people who eat little or no meat. In these groups, an A1C in the prediabetes range might reflect iron status as much as glucose.

If someone's A1C doesn't line up with their fasting glucose or glucose monitor readings, it's worth checking iron status before concluding that blood sugar is the problem.

Statins & Dementia: What Happened When They Stopped (Then Restarted) the Drugs
In a 2012 pilot study (Padala et al., American Journal of Geriatric Pharmacotherapy), researchers took 18 older adults with Alzheimer’s who were already on statins and ran a simple test:
•  Stopped the statins for 6 weeks
•  Restarted them for another 6 weeks
What they found:
•  Cognition improved when the statins were stopped (MMSE scores rose ~1.9 points, P = 0.014).
•  Cognition worsened again when the statins were restarted (MMSE dropped ~1.9 points, P = 0.007).
•  Cholesterol rose off the drug and fell when it was restarted (as expected).
•  There were also trends toward better daily function (ADL/IADL) while off the statins.
The authors concluded that statins may adversely affect cognition in people with dementia. This was a small, open-label pilot (not a large randomized controlled trial), so it doesn’t prove causation for everyone—but the withdrawal/rechallenge design makes the signal hard to ignore.
Cholesterol is critical for brain function. Some statins (especially lipophilic ones) can cross the blood-brain barrier and may interfere with that. The FDA has long noted reversible cognitive side effects with statins.
This doesn’t mean every patient should stop their statin. It does raise the question of whether continued use is always the right call in someone already dealing with dementia—especially if the original indication was primary prevention. 
Source: Padala KP et al. Am J Geriatr Pharmacother. 2012;10(5):296-302. PMID: 22921881
